title: Isaac Io Schankler: Orb Pondering Simulator LIVE!
speaker: Isaac Io Schankler
summary: Composer Isaac Io Schankler stages 'Orb Pondering Simulator', a live, staged-to-go-wrong audiovisual performance framed as a box-breathing exercise with a growing and shrinking orb whose sound swells with it. After a scripted 'lockout', the audience is invited to type debug commands (!spawn, !kill) in chat, which spawn non-orb objects and ERROR entities and eventually lead to two alternate endings ('spawn everybody' and 'kill everybody'). In Q&A Schankler explains the inspirations (live electronic concerts going wrong, an earlier Twitch-controlled modular synth) and the deliberate reduction to a tiny command vocabulary so everyone could participate. There is little roguelike design content; it is mainly an example of audience-participatory procedural audio performance.

insights.claim: Crowd-controlled interactive performances work better with a very small, simple command set, because intricate commands let only a handful of people participate.
insights.detail: Schankler's earlier project, the Public Modular, let people play a modular synth remotely through Twitch chat commands; it was fun but its complicated commands meant only a few people could get a handle on it. For Orb Pondering Simulator they stripped commands down to a simple set like !spawn and !kill.
insights.quote: only a handful of people could were like able to like get a handle on it and actually participate in it

insights.claim: Orb Pondering Simulator ties a sound's loudness directly to an orb's size to pace box breathing: breathe in as it grows, hold while it holds, breathe out as it shrinks.
insights.detail: Schankler presents it as based on breathing exercises that calm and focus the mind. In Q&A they note that the ERROR entities breathe at a different rate, so following them could make you hyperventilate.
insights.quote: there's a sound that gets louder as the orb grows and quieter as the orb shrinks

insights.claim: Orb Pondering Simulator hides two alternate endings behind the same small verb set ('spawn everybody' vs 'kill everybody'), so which ending a crowd reaches depends on what it tries first.
insights.detail: Schankler says they were curious which command people would reach first and were happy the audience found 'spawn everybody' first; 'kill everybody' was shown afterwards as the bad ending. The host praised how failure states like killing a non-existent orb became their own inputs, spawning errors, like creative inputs in text games.
insights.quote: there are as you may have guessed two kind of alternate endings um spawn everybody and kill everybody
